finding: The recipe's own check block (unfold.awk and unfold.py extract the same 20-line script, cmp'd) runs the mods tool, planted-fault proofs, books check, taxonomy shape and the no-em-dash rule, so the file proves itself and an agent handed it can verify without a human.
falsifier: Running `awk -f tools/unfold.awk RECIPE.org` and `python3 tools/unfold.py RECIPE.org` gives differing output, or `sh` on it fails (I ran the cmp: identical, 20 lines).

finding: Errata section prints seven real mistakes each beside what caught it; erratum 7 (Ap_MedallionOpens stand-in would have sealed Misery Mire and Turtle Rock) is verified by src/mods_off.c line 192 holding the original rule, which is exactly the trust a modder needs.
falsifier: src/mods_off.c line 192 does not hold the medallion rule, or no other erratum matches a commit.

finding: The tool is Python and its tests are shell, and --prove-red plants eight faults that all turn red (I ran it: 8 RED lines), which matches the RECIPE's stated count and the lab's separate-language rule.
falsifier: Running `sh tests/mods/run.sh --prove-red | grep -c 'RED as'` printed something other than 8, or any line says STILL GREEN.

finding: The claim 'RECIPE > versioning, consistency of voice > tone of voice' is stated and left to 'time will judge'; the branch could take it by adding one measurable check (for example a tests/books gauge that both books use the same route phrases 'Turn to §N' and 'Back to', which they already do) so the claim has a number, not a promise.
falsifier: A grep shows the two books do not share those route phrases, or the reader states a number is unwanted for this claim.

finding: Voice is consistent where it counts: both books open with 'Who is talking', first person singular, 'turn to §N' routes and a closing section naming what was left out, so a reader can tell the two seats apart yet hear one author; but RECIPE.org speaks of Corwin in third person and README in plain project voice, so the claim holds between the books and is only partly shown across the branch.
falsifier: A reader given one paragraph from each of RECIPE.org, manual.md and devguide.md picks the author of all three without hesitation.

finding: The mods block in RECIPE.org (line 72) is empty and the devguide teaches from-recipe, but nothing shows an agent the finished loop for the common ask 'build me a copy without 3D and Archipelago', so a one-line worked prompt-to-block example in the RECIPE would let an agent hand-off be copied rather than inferred.
falsifier: An agent given only RECIPE.org and that sentence produces `-hd3d -archipelago` in the block and a good `mods.py check` on first try without the example.

finding: Section 14 tells a couch host to run `zelda3 --mods` from a terminal, but the build already refuses mismatches with 'Different game version or mods' (session.c:816); the branch could show the mod list in the join-refusal message or in the menu so the player never needs a terminal.
falsifier: A player in a refused join sees which mods differ without running a command, or session.c's message cannot carry text.

finding: The catalog, spec and stand-ins make each mod's surface a declared thing, which the upstream maintainer could take as a bare minimum: a 'mods.py guard' step in CI (build.yaml already runs books build) would keep every future contribution guarded at no cost to him.
falsifier: build.yaml already runs `tools/mods.py guard`, or guard fails on a clean tree (it printed nothing and exited 0 for me).

finding: The ground section says 'SKIP helpbook' appears in the stock run, a visible on-ramp showing the skip rule; the branch could also state what a Windows or macOS reader sees in place of `sh tests/...`, since the recipe is shell-only and the books promise Windows help.
falsifier: A Windows reader can follow every RECIPE command without WSL, MinGW or a shell.

finding: Best manual section is §1: it counts six routes, then tests whether one failure closes all six (your own ROM) and collapses them to one road, so the player's first page gives the single fact that prevents the commonest dead end and hands out three routes by readiness.
falsifier: A player with a ROM but no build still ends at §15 without finding the ROM requirement first.

finding: Weakest manual section is §14 (Which mods your copy has): it is the one player page that speaks in build terms, with a terminal command and 'game-changing mods', and ends by sending the player off to the other book.
falsifier: A couch-host reader finds the section answers 'can we play together tonight' in under three lines.

finding: Best devguide section is §15 (Errata, printed beside the error): each entry gives symptom, catcher and lesson, and it converts the branch's history into a modder's checklist rather than a story.
falsifier: A modder skipping §15 hits one of the seven errors listed without being warned elsewhere in the guide.

finding: Weakest devguide section is §16 (The recipe, and the models behind it): two paragraphs of pointers with no command, no expected output and no worked step, in a book whose other sections end on one; it is the section an agent reads to learn how the whole was built and gets a directory listing.
falsifier: §16 contains a command and a stated expectation, or a reader finds it enough to rebuild the branch's checks.

id: Prose: I ran `python3 tools/mods.py check`, `python3 tools/books.py check`, `sh tests/books/run.sh`, `sh tests/mods/run.sh`, `--prove-red` and the RECIPE unfold comparison; all passed and nothing in the tree changed. The only dirty file is get_python_libs.bat, which predates this review. The branch's claims about M1 to M21 and eight planted faults check out against the files. The main reach gap is the headline claim (RECIPE over versioning, voice over tone) being asserted without any check, though the books do share one voice. Windows readers get books and a build path but the RECIPE commands assume a shell. I did not run the matrix, coop tests or ./zelda3 as instructed, so the 103-function census figure in devguide §3 is unverified by me.
